newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat takes Hebron, assures Jewish settlers.
newsitem.headline: Arafat takes Hebron, assures Jewish settlers.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat took control of most of Hebron on Sunday telling Jewish settlers who remain at the heart of the divided city he wanted peace.

Arafat laid claim to Hebron, the prize of months of bitter negotiations with Israel's right-wing leader Benjamin Netanyahu, in a speech to 25,000 supporters on a hill above the city, revered by Jews and Moslems as Abraham's burial place.
"I tell settlers we do not want confrontation," the former guerrilla chief said, having flown by helicopter to the hilltop headquarters of Israel's 30-year-long occupation that ended on Friday.
"It's all empty words, empty slogans. Our city's been abandoned," said David Wilder, a spokesman for the armed settlers who live in the one fifth of Hebron that remains in Israeli hands.
"Now the city of Hebron is a liberated city," Arafat told an enthusiastic crowd that surged forward preventing him from reviewing an honour guard.

Arafat said Hebron was a launching pad for further Israeli withdrawals in the West Bank. He said Israel would release Palestinian women prisoners in a few days followed by the eventual release of Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, the spiritual leader of the Islamic fundamentalist Hamas movement.
"Hebron is a springboard for what comes after...so that we can establish our independent Palestinian state," Arafat said in Arabic.
"A promise is a promise, we will continue to Jerusalem," he added to applause.
Arafat has made the same promise about making Arab East Jerusalem his capital in every Palestinian town he has "liberated" since arriving in Gaza in July 1994 to lead the self-rule Authority.

The Hebron agreement, reached after much arm-twisting by the United States, has revived hopes that Arafat and Prime Minister Netanyahu can see the wider self-rule accord through to a final resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including issues like settlements and Jerusalem, in 1999.

"Peace has now been settled with all Israelis," Arafat told Reuters after meeting dignitaries at Hebron City Hall. He was referring to the approval of the Hebron deal last Thursday by both right and left wing parties in Israel's parliament.
Arafat broke the Moslem Ramadan fast with Hebron residents. He was scheduled to leave for Gaza later.
Hebron's hilly streets were adorned with Palestinian flags and posters of the man called "Abu Ammar".
Arafat's stubbled jowls smiled down from a mural erected on a hill overlooking the enclaves where some 400 Jews live and study in the heart of the town of 100,000 Palestinians.
There were few settlers on the streets to witness the celebrations for a man they call a murderer. They see Palestinian self-rule as a betrayal of their biblical right to all of the West Bank.
Both Arab and Jew fear violence from each other in Hebron where some 2,000 Israeli soldiers will stay to protect the settlers.
"If these Jewish settlers in Hebron who have been provocative to Palestinians here do not make problems there will be no problems in Hebron," said West Bank Palestinian security chief Jibril Rajoub.
The Israeli security establishment and settlers were up in arms on Sunday over Rajoub's remarks on Saturday that the settlers did not belong in Hebron.
"I said Hebron was not a natural place for these settlers and I stick by that," Rajoub told Reuters.
"These are harsh words of incitement and verbal violence that constitute a gross violation of the agreement that Jibril Rajoub personally played a part in achieving," an Israeli security source said.

Rajoub, a native of Hebron, is in overall charge of the 400 uniformed police and 500 plainclothes police who officially deployed in Hebron after the last Israeli soldiers slipped away at dawn on Friday.
But PLO sources said many more Palestinian security men were in the city with Israel's tacit approval. The sources said Rajoub would move his headquarters to Hebron from Jericho.

Rajoub, whose forces have been accused of human rights violations by civil rights groups, told Reuters: "We will punish any Palestinian who violates the law and any policeman who maltreats Palestinians will also be punished."
